alignments.note: One connective morpheme rendered by a coordinator and a subordinator written together at the clause's left edge, which rule 55 makes one rendering. The morpheme is itself a subordinator, so the head goes on 'though', which writes its own force, exactly as rule 55's 'for though' example directs; 'For' as head was the competing reading.
Predicate of a verbless clause; the construction-supplied copula joins it under rule 20, headed on the word carrying the lexeme.
Explicit subject takes only its own English (rule 20).
The waw takes the connective written for it, 'yet' (rule 14's open list).
Anarthrous substantival adjective takes the English supplied to make it a noun phrase (rule 46), headed on the word carrying the lexeme.

Light verb with complement, headed on 'respect' (rule 44); the supplied 'unto' is what the English verb needs to reach its own bare object and joins the verb's unit under rule 44's supplied-preposition clause.
The waw takes the adversative 'But' written for it (rule 14).
Anarthrous substantival adjective with its supplied 'the' (rule 46).
Preposition rendered 'from'; the noun keeps a word of its own, so rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet and rule 2 splits the pair.
Finite verb with its subject pronoun (rule 17); the fronted object stands between under rule 25.

review_notes: The pair 'For though' is read as one rendering of the single kî under rule 55, headed on the subordinating word; the alternative head is named in that unit's note.
'from afar' is split rather than fused, each morpheme holding a word of its own.
